---
title: "Missing values"
---

{{< include ../_setup.qmd >}}

```{r}
#| include: false
patchy <- god_table("patchy")
contacts <- god_table("contacts")
sensors <- god_table("sensors")
hourly <- god_table("hourly")
logged <- god_table("logged")
```

```{python}
#| include: false
patchy = god_table("patchy")
contacts = god_table("contacts")
sensors = god_table("sensors")
hourly = god_table("hourly")
logged = god_table("logged")
```

What should a hole in the table mean for your answer? `drop_missing` drops
rows where a named column is missing. With no column named, it looks at
every column.

The table is `patchy`, three products with one revenue that never arrived:

```{r}
#| echo: false
patchy
```

::: {.panel-tabset}

### run

```{r}
run('
  patchy
    then drop_missing [revenue]
')
```

### R

```{r}
patchy |> drop_missing(revenue)
```

### Python

```{python}
patchy >> drop_missing(col.revenue)
```

:::

*`patchy then drop_missing [revenue]`*

`fill_missing` replaces missing values with something.

::: {.panel-tabset}

### run

```{r}
run('
  patchy
    then fill_missing [revenue] as 0
')
```

### R

```{r}
patchy |> fill_missing(revenue = 0)
```

### Python

```{python}
patchy >> fill_missing(revenue = 0)
```

:::

The filler has to be the same kind of thing the column holds, or the column would
quietly stop being what it was.

::: {.panel-tabset}

### R

```{r}
#| error: true
patchy |> fill_missing(revenue = "none") |> collect()
```

### Python

```{python}
#| classes: refusal
try:
    collect(patchy >> fill_missing(revenue = "none"))
except GodError as refusal:
    print(refusal)
```

:::

## Taking the first column that has a value

`fill_missing` puts one value in every gap. When the value you want is in another
column, `first_present` reads across the columns you name and takes the first one
that is there.

`contacts` holds three ways of reaching someone and not everybody has all three:

```{r}
#| echo: false
contacts
```

::: {.panel-tabset}

### run

```{r}
run('
  contacts
    then add [reach] as first_present([mobile], [landline], [email])
')
```

### R

```{r}
contacts |> add(reach = first_present(mobile, landline, email))
```

### Python

```{python}
contacts >> add(reach = first_present(col.mobile, col.landline, col.email))
```

:::

*`contacts then add [reach] as first_present([mobile], [landline], [email])`*

Two things about it surprise people, and both matter before you rely on it.

The order is a priority rather than a set. It reads left to right and stops at the
first column that has a value, so ana is reached on the mobile number even though
a landline and an email are there too. Writing the same three columns in another
order gives a different answer, which is the point of writing them in an order at
all.

The only thing it skips is a missing value. A zero, an empty text and a `no`
are all values, and they come back. `sensors` holds a reading and its backup
for two sensors:

```{r}
#| echo: false
sensors
```

::: {.panel-tabset}

### run

```{r}
run('
  sensors
    then add [used] as first_present([sensor], [backup])
')
```

### R

```{r}
sensors |> add(used = first_present(sensor, backup))
```

### Python

```{python}
sensors >> add(used = first_present(col.sensor, col.backup))
```

:::

*`sensors then add [used] as first_present([sensor], [backup])`*

The first sensor read zero, which is a reading, so it is kept. Only the row
where the sensor recorded nothing at all takes its value from the backup. If
you want zero treated as missing too, say so in a step of its own, because
that is a decision about your data rather than about the word.

Every column it looks in has to hold the same kind of thing, since one of them is
going to be the answer and a column holds one kind. If all of them are missing
for a row, the answer for that row is missing.

SQL and dplyr both call this `coalesce`. It is `first_present` here because
`missing` is already the grammar's word for the absent value, so `present` is
its opposite. And `first` names the part people most often misread: the
columns are a priority order.

## Carrying the last value forward

A reading taken hourly, where the sensor only reports when the value changes,
leaves holes that are not really missing: the value is the last one you saw.
`latest` fills a hole with the most recent value above it.

The table is `hourly`, one sensor with holes where it did not report:

```{r}
#| echo: false
hourly
```

::: {.panel-tabset}

### run

```{r}
run('
  hourly
    then sort [taken_at]
    then add [reading] as latest([reading])
', hourly = hourly)
```

### R

```{r}
hourly |> sort(taken_at) |> add(reading = latest(reading))
```

### Python

```{python}
hourly >> sort(col.taken_at) >> add(reading = latest(col.reading))
```

:::

*`hourly then sort [taken_at] then add [reading] as latest([reading])`*

It fills a run of holes, not just one. That is the difference between this
and reaching for `previous`, which looks back exactly one row and leaves the
second hole of a pair still open.

Like every value that walks the rows, it needs a `sort` first, because "the
last value" means nothing until something has said last in what order. And
`by` restarts it for each group, so one group never borrows another's value.
`logged` holds two sensors, each with holes of its own:

```{r}
#| echo: false
logged
```

::: {.panel-tabset}

### run

```{r}
run('
  logged
    then sort [sensor], [taken_at]
    then add [reading] as latest([reading]) by [sensor]
', logged = logged)
```

### R

```{r}
logged |>
  sort(sensor, taken_at) |>
  add(reading = latest(reading), by = sensor)
```

### Python

```{python}
(logged
  >> sort(col.sensor, col.taken_at)
  >> add(reading = latest(col.reading), by = col.sensor))
```

:::

A row with nothing above it and nothing of its own stays missing, because
there is no earlier value to carry. `fill_missing` after it puts a value
there if you want one.

## Where the holes go when you sort

Holes arrive on their own once you join two tables. `join` is taught in [the
next chapter](another-table.qmd); here it is only where the holes come from.
`sales` sells a Sprocket and `products` has never heard of one, so joining
them leaves rows whose `maker` nobody recorded:

::: {.panel-tabset}

### run

```{r}
run('
  sales
    then join products by [product]
    then summarize [total] as total([revenue]) by [maker]
    then sort [maker]
')
```

### R

```{r}
sales |>
  join(products, by = product) |>
  summarize(total = total(revenue), by = maker) |>
  sort(maker)
```

### Python

```{python}
(sales
  >> join(products, by = col.product)
  >> summarize(total = total(col.revenue), by = col.maker)
  >> sort(col.maker))
```

:::

*`sales then join products by [product] then summarize [total] as total([revenue]) by [maker] then sort [maker]`*

Sorting raises a question the sort itself does not answer: the row with no maker
has nothing to be ordered by, so where does it go? The grammar's answer is
*last*, and you get it without asking. Reading it aloud is the reason: the
values you have, then the ones you do not. It stays last when you reverse the
sort, too. `descending` reverses the values, and a row with no value has nothing
to reverse.

When you want the holes first, say so. `missing first` goes after the keys,
because it applies to the whole sort rather than to one of them:

::: {.panel-tabset}

### run

```{r}
run('
  sales
    then join products by [product]
    then summarize [total] as total([revenue]) by [maker]
    then sort [maker] missing first
')
```

### R

```{r}
sales |>
  join(products, by = product) |>
  summarize(total = total(revenue), by = maker) |>
  sort(maker, missing = "first")
```

### Python

```{python}
(sales
  >> join(products, by = col.product)
  >> summarize(total = total(col.revenue), by = col.maker)
  >> sort(col.maker, missing = "first"))
```

:::

*`sales then join products by [product] then summarize [total] as total([revenue]) by [maker] then sort [maker] missing first`*

This is a place where the tools underneath genuinely disagree, and the grammar
picks one answer for all of them. By default, DuckDB, dplyr and pandas put the
absent rows last; polars puts them first; Spark puts them first going up and
last coming down. The same question, five tools, three answers. So every tool
that would put them anywhere else is told where they go. The sentence means the
same thing wherever it runs, which is the whole of what this grammar is for.

## The same answer, wherever an order is read

A sort settles more than the row order. Anything that reads the rows *in* that
order reads them the way the sort left them, so `row_number` counts the row with
no maker where the sort put it, which is last:

::: {.panel-tabset}

### run

```{r}
run('
  sales
    then join products by [product]
    then summarize [total] as total([revenue]) by [maker]
    then sort [maker]
    then add [place] as row_number()
')
```

### R

```{r}
sales |>
  join(products, by = product) |>
  summarize(total = total(revenue), by = maker) |>
  sort(maker) |>
  add(place = row_number())
```

### Python

```{python}
(sales
  >> join(products, by = col.product)
  >> summarize(total = total(col.revenue), by = col.maker)
  >> sort(col.maker)
  >> add(place = row_number()))
```

:::

*`sales then join products by [product] then summarize [total] as total([revenue]) by [maker] then sort [maker] then add [place] as row_number()`*

Say `missing first` and the counting moves with it, because it is the same
order being read:

::: {.panel-tabset}

### run

```{r}
run('
  sales
    then join products by [product]
    then summarize [total] as total([revenue]) by [maker]
    then sort [maker] missing first
    then add [place] as row_number()
')
```

### R

```{r}
sales |>
  join(products, by = product) |>
  summarize(total = total(revenue), by = maker) |>
  sort(maker, missing = "first") |>
  add(place = row_number())
```

### Python

```{python}
(sales
  >> join(products, by = col.product)
  >> summarize(total = total(col.revenue), by = col.maker)
  >> sort(col.maker, missing = "first")
  >> add(place = row_number()))
```

:::

*`sales then join products by [product] then summarize [total] as total([revenue]) by [maker] then sort [maker] missing first then add [place] as row_number()`*

`previous`, `running_total`, `latest` and a grouped `take` all read that same
line, and all of them move with it. The rule is worth stating once: a window
frames the way the sort above it framed, holes and all.

## When a window reads the hole

A window can also read the value in the hole, and then the question is what it
answers there. `running_total` and `rank` both answer missing on that row:

::: {.panel-tabset}

### run

```{r}
run('
  patchy
    then sort [product]
    then add [so_far] as running_total([revenue]), [place] as rank([revenue] descending)
')
```

### R

```{r}
patchy |>
  sort(product) |>
  add(so_far = running_total(revenue), place = rank(descending(revenue)))
```

### Python

```{python}
(patchy
  >> sort(col.product)
  >> add(so_far = running_total(col.revenue),
         place = rank(descending(col.revenue))))
```

:::

*`patchy then sort [product] then add [so_far] as running_total([revenue]), [place] as rank([revenue] descending)`*

Gadget's revenue never arrived, so it has no place among the others, and no
total so far either. Repeating Doohickey's 300 on its row would say that
Gadget added nothing, which nobody knows. The hole changes no other row:
Widget's total counts the two revenues that are there, and the two of them are
ranked first and second. pandas and polars answer this way already. SQL would
rank the hole last and repeat the total, and R's `cumsum` would carry the hole
to every row below it, so the grammar says which it means.
